currentContext.business: Sanathan Textiles manufactures yarn across three largely unrelated verticals: polyester filament yarn (made through a fully integrated setup that converts raw material into polyester chips and then into yarn), finer-count compact cotton yarn, and specialised yarns for technical textiles engineered for high durability and tenacity. The Company sells through an extensive agent-based distribution network in India and international markets, serving apparel, home textile, automotive, defence, logistics, travel and sports/athleisure customers. It is transitioning from a predominantly single-location operation at Silvassa to a multi-location footprint spanning Silvassa and Wazirabad, Punjab, with the Punjab plant run through wholly owned subsidiary Sanathan Polycot Private Limited.

Cotton Yarn: Cotton Combed Compact Yarn (finer counts 36s to 61s)
Value-added / specialty yarns: Sanathan Reviro (recycled yarn from recycled PET waste)

currentContext.strengths: Three verticals with largely unrelated demand drivers - polyester economics track PTA/MEG and crude, cotton follows an agricultural rhythm, technical textiles follow industrial activity and safety regulation - so the cycles tend to offset one another and steady the earnings base|Full forward and backward integration in polyester, converting raw material into chips and then yarn, giving control of quality at the polymer stage, a wider product portfolio from the same asset base, faster sampling and retention of value that would otherwise accrue to intermediate suppliers|Distribution depth built over two decades - 300+ agents across 17 Indian states plus an international network, 1400+ customers serviced and 50,000+ SKUs - which let new Punjab capacity be placed through channels that already existed rather than building market and plant simultaneously|Value-added and specification yarns (cationic dyeable, born dyed, stretch, moisture-wicking, recycled Reviro) sold on relationship and consistency rather than day-to-day price, including protective-equipment applications where qualification takes an extended period|Punjab plant removes a structural freight, lead-time and working-capital disadvantage for North Indian buyers previously served over long distances; Silvassa's proximity to western ports serves export and imported feedstock flows|Automation across doffing, warehousing, material handling and packaging with digital process controls and real-time quality monitoring, supporting cost optimisation at scale|Demand-led capacity sequencing - capacity built against demand already identified, which the Company credits for holding utilisation through demand shocks, feedstock volatility and disrupted logistics
currentContext.strategies: Transition from a predominantly single-location operation at Silvassa to a multi-location footprint spanning Silvassa and Wazirabad, Punjab, with Punjab established as a dedicated supply hub for the North India textile ecosystem and materially shorter lead times to garment clusters such as Delhi, NCR, Haryana, Amritsar, Punjab, Ludhiana and Panipat|Scale the Punjab polyester filament yarn facility in phases toward its full potential, with Phase II planned for commissioning by the end of FY27|Build out technical textiles as the next growth vertical by doubling Silvassa capacity from 9,000 MTPA to 18,000 MTPA, with plant and machinery already in place and commercial production to commence soon|Progress a proposed new cotton yarn manufacturing facility in Madhya Pradesh|Shift the portfolio toward value-added, specification yarns (cationic dyeable, born-dyed, moisture-wicking and specialised technical textile yarns) on the stated view that commodity yarn is a price business while specification yarn is a relationship business|Maintain a diversified three-vertical presence - polyester filament, cotton and technical textiles - because each addresses distinct end markets and demand cycles (petrochemical, agricultural, industrial/infrastructure), giving resilience across market conditions|Immediate priority is to optimise and improve the efficiency of the expanded manufacturing platform while driving higher capacity utilisation and operational efficiency|Proactive procurement to insulate operations from feedstock price fluctuations, elevated freight costs and geopolitical disruption - timely sourcing of PTA and MEG, calibrated inventory planning and long-standing supplier partnerships across Silvassa and Punjab|Run an integrated operating model linking procurement, manufacturing and distribution, using the distribution network for early visibility of market requirements to optimise inventory deployment and accelerate product development|Embed sustainability into manufacturing from the outset at Punjab - agri waste as renewable heating fuel, Zero Liquid Discharge treatment of all process water, operation in accordance with the Global Recycled Standard, plus OEKO-TEX and ISO certifications, and pallet packing that removes carton usage from despatch to the extent possible|Develop value-added yarns that reduce customers' own environmental impact, such as born-dyed yarn which eliminates the conventional dyeing stage and removes an entire wet processing step downstream|Retain and reinvest profits rather than pay a dividend, funding the Punjab, Silvassa and Madhya Pradesh expansion|Continue investing in automation, digital process controls and advanced quality monitoring, with forward and backward integration and partnerships with recognised global manufacturers
currentContext.expansion: FY 2025-26 was the year Sanathan Textiles moved from a predominantly single-location operation at Silvassa to a two-plant footprint. The greenfield polyester filament yarn facility at Wazirabad, Punjab - built and operated through the wholly owned subsidiary Sanathan Polycot Private Limited - had its continuous polymerisation line commissioned on August 27, 2025, was ramped up and stabilised at 700 MTPD, and registered that maximum capacity in the last week of March 2026, completing Phase 1 at 255,500 MTPA of polyester yarn capacity on an 80-acre site. The Company describes this as the most significant operational milestone in its history and as its first expansion of this scale accomplished in a single step; it was preceded by years of study of the North Indian textile ecosystem, and the plant is positioned to remove the freight, lead-time and working-capital disadvantage that North Indian buyers previously bore when served over long distances. Silvassa, a 50-acre site with 21 years of operation, continues to run its integrated polyester, cotton and technical-textile lines at optimal utilisation, serving domestic and export demand through proximity to India's western ports. The Company frames the journey as one from 4,500 MTPA to 479,250 MTPA built over two decades of demand-led, incremental capacity creation - understanding the market first and building second. Three further steps are disclosed in the capacity status table: an additional 9,000 MTPA of technical textiles at Silvassa where plant and machinery is installed and commissioning is pending; Phase 2 at Punjab adding 91,250 MTPA of polyester yarn capacity; and 73,000 spindles of cotton yarn capacity in Madhya Pradesh, both listed as upcoming capacity expansion. On completion of Phase 2 the Company expects aggregate installed capacity to increase substantially and polyester filament yarn capacity to more than double over the coming years. The Directors state that the peak-investment phase has largely been completed and that no dividend was recommended because capital is being deployed across the Punjab, Silvassa and Madhya Pradesh projects. Alongside capacity, investment continues in automation - automated warehousing, material handling and packing, process control, digital quality monitoring - which the Company argues is a precondition for holding its cost position at this scale, and in sustainable infrastructure: ZLD systems and rice husk / agricultural-waste biomass-fired heaters at Punjab, planned solar power initiatives, and dedicated investments in renewable generation capacity said to be at an advanced stage, with the Punjab biomass model being evaluated for replication across other sites. No rupee capex quantum is stated: the capital-commitments disclosure in this bundle is only a cross-reference to another note and carries no figure.
currentContext.mdna: As utilisation improves, management expects stronger operating leverage, better absorption of fixed costs and a corresponding improvement in margins|Having largely completed the peak-investment phase, the Company expects operating leverage from higher utilisation, backward integration and a progressively cleaner, lower-cost energy mix to support margins and cash flows as the new assets mature|The Punjab commissioning raised depreciation and finance costs, temporarily impacting consolidated profitability; management frames these as transitional effects of a business that has fundamentally become stronger, with standalone operations continuing to deliver steady growth|Incremental volumes from Punjab were absorbed across the North Indian textile market during the year, broadening the customer base and improving responsiveness across key textile clusters|Structural shift in the fibre mix toward man-made fibres, with the Government's National Fibre Scheme seeking to rebalance India's fibre mix by 2030-31 - said to augur well for a company with capabilities across both cotton and man-made fibre yarns|Business sentiment strengthened during the second half of FY26, particularly across export-oriented segments such as garments and home textiles, and exports of man-made yarn, fabrics and made-ups increased|Improving export sentiment, favourable trade agreements and continued diversification of global sourcing towards India are expected to support sustained industry growth|Near-term outlook aided by supportive policy, including the temporary exemption of raw cotton imports from customs duty and the Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Cess, and improving trade access for Indian textiles|Polyester filament yarn is the dominant revenue driver, contributing 82% of revenue in the year, with technical textiles described as currently a smaller part of the portfolio but a significant growth opportunity|Silvassa's proximity to India's western ports serves imported feedstock and export shipments, while Punjab serves North India through shorter lead times and logistics efficiency|Directors remain confident in the medium-term growth trajectory while recognising that outcomes remain subject to raw-material and energy-cost volatility and to global trade and tariff developments|Externally, elevated tariffs imposed by the United States created stress for Indian manufacturers, particularly exporters, and trade fragmentation and geopolitical tension (including the conflict in West Asia) remain sources of near-term uncertainty

risks.note: Identified in the BRSR material-issues table as both risk and opportunity: increasing frequency and severity of extreme weather events is a direct operational risk to manufacturing continuity and supply chain stability, and to the availability and quality of cotton - a climate-sensitive and substantially rain-fed crop - and may elevate compliance and operational costs across the textile value chain. Mitigation cited: technology upgrades for energy efficiency, expanding renewable energy generation capacity, biomass-fired heaters running on agricultural waste at the Punjab facility with evaluation of replicating that model at other sites, and diversification of raw-material origin.

risks.risk: Water stress, water-intensive operations and tightening effluent regulation
risks.note: Manufacturing is water-intensive and downstream customers are heavily water-dependent in dyeing, printing and processing. Climate-induced water stress in key operating geographies combined with tightening regulatory norms on industrial water use and effluent discharge is described as a material risk to operational continuity and licence to operate; most of the water footprint embodied in cotton yarn arises upstream in cultivation. Mitigation: Zero Liquid Discharge and resource circularity, rainwater harvesting and direct drawl of fresh water from alternative sources to reduce groundwater reliance, and dope-dyed yarns that cut water use at the customer's stage.

Flagged as a risk in the BRSR material-issues table: improper handling of hazardous and non-hazardous waste streams threatens human health and the environment, with potential consequences including regulatory penalties, litigation and reputational damage. Mitigation is a systematic framework of source segregation and resource recovery, strictly categorising hazardous and non-hazardous waste streams.

risks.risk: Raw material and energy cost volatility
risks.note: The forward-looking-statement caution names movements in raw material and energy costs among the factors that could cause actual results to differ materially. The BRSR climate row reinforces the exposure, framing energy-efficiency and renewable investment as a way of lowering operating costs and insulating margins from volatility in fuel and electricity prices - with upfront capital investment required and returns realised only over the medium term.

risks.risk: Raw material sourcing and cotton procurement exposure
risks.note: Cotton is a climate-sensitive, substantially rain-fed crop and its availability and quality are cited as directly at risk. The Company relies on a structural hedge - integrated presence across cotton, polyester and technical textiles - plus a diversified cotton procurement base with supplier relationships spanning Asia, South America, North America and Australia to keep input supply steady.

risks.risk: Trade policy, tariffs and geopolitical disruption
risks.note: Elevated tariffs imposed by the United States created stress for Indian manufacturers, particularly exporters, and weighed on business confidence during the year. Trade fragmentation, tariff-related disruption and geopolitical tension are expected to intermittently weigh on exports and investor sentiment, and the conflict in West Asia introduced fresh uncertainty with potential to affect energy markets, supply chains and the cost of energy-intensive commodities. Trade fragmentation and tariff realignment across major consuming markets are named as a near-term uncertainty for the global textile industry.

risks.risk: Demand and pricing volatility in domestic and international markets
risks.note: The cautionary statement names changes in economic conditions and in demand and pricing in the domestic and international markets in which the Company operates as factors that could cause outcomes to differ materially from stated expectations - a structural exposure for a yarn manufacturer selling across both domestic and export channels.

risks.risk: Regulatory, tax and legal change, and labour relations
risks.note: Changes in Government regulations, tax regimes and trade policy, litigation and labour relations are enumerated in the forward-looking-statement caution as factors outside the Company's control that could materially change outcomes; tightening industrial water-use and effluent norms are a live example of the regulatory direction described elsewhere in the report.

thesis (one line): Recently-IPO'd multi-fibre yarn maker (Silvassa anchor + new Punjab subsidiary) in a transition year: Punjab Phase-1 ramped to full only by end-Mar'26, so consol margins are temporarily depressed by depreciation/interest; FY27 should show steep operating-leverage recovery (EBITDA guided to ~2x) as Punjab stabilizes, technical-textile capacity doubles, and the value-added mix climbs.

**Consolidated (incl. Punjab subsidiary):**
| Metric | Q4 FY26 | YoY | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | INR 1,169.2 cr | +59.7% YoY, +8.4% QoQ | Punjab subsidiary now contributing |
| EBITDA | INR 94.4 cr | +38.1% YoY, +65% QoQ (vs INR 57.2 cr Q3) | margin 8.1% vs 5.3% Q3 FY26 |
| PAT (rptd) | INR 21.6 cr | — | depressed by Punjab depreciation + finance cost |

**Standalone (Silvassa):**
| Metric | Q4 FY26 | YoY | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | INR 752.8 cr | +3% (vs 731.2 cr) | full-capacity Silvassa |
| EBITDA | INR 82.5 cr | +16.9% (vs 70.6 cr) | margin 11% vs 9.7% Q4 FY25, 7% Q3 FY26 |
| PAT | INR 56.0 cr | +12.3% (vs 49.9 cr) | |

**FY26 full-year:** Consol rev INR 3,811.2 cr (+27.1% vs 2,996.6 cr); Consol EBITDA INR 284.4 cr (vs 263.5 cr); Consol PAT INR 77.3 cr. Standalone rev INR 3,037.9 cr (vs 2,996.8); Standalone EBITDA INR 277.1 cr (margin 9.1% vs 8.9%); Standalone PAT INR 191.9 cr (+10%).

**Volume:** Silvassa FY26 production 2.31 lakh MT, sales 2.28 lakh MT. **Value-added mix:** Silvassa >40% value-addition achieved; Punjab started at ~10%, intends to scale up.
**Net debt:** ~INR 1,325 cr (Mar'26 exit). **Gross debt:** ~INR 1,500 cr (peak); cost of debt ~7.25% (incl. PTA/MEG LC payables beyond 68 days).
**One-offs / non-recurring:** raw material in transit of ~INR 180 cr inflated inventory & sundry creditors; payable days rose 59→104 (mgmt says will normalize as full-quarter COGS base builds). Gas cost at Silvassa up ~50-60% (gas = ~6-7% of operational cost).
guidance (critical):
- **Revenue FY27:** Silvassa ~INR 3,100 cr (vs ~3,000 FY26); Punjab ~INR 2,600 cr → **consol ~INR 5,600-5,700 cr**.
- **EBITDA FY27:** "north of INR 500 cr" (vs ~280 cr FY26) — i.e. nearly doubling; targets **double-digit consol EBITDA margin** (currently single digit; conservative given global situation). Tracks business on **EBITDA per ton** (if prices rise, % falls but per-ton holds).
- **PBT FY27:** ~INR 225-250 cr (after Punjab interest + depreciation; consol finance cost to stay north of INR 125 cr; depreciation run-rate ~INR 120 cr).
- **Capacity / capex:** Technical-yarn at Silvassa doubling 9,000 → 18,000 MTPA, commissioning **end of Q1 FY27 (July)**, adds ~INR 150 cr revenue. Punjab **Phase 2** targeted commission **end-FY28** (clarified, not FY27), takes Punjab to >INR 4,000 cr revenue. **Cotton expansion** in MP (Dhar, PM MITRA scheme): 50 acres bought (paid INR 26 cr), 72,000 spindles, possession by last quarter CY26, production ~10-12 months later → revenue from **H2 FY28**, adds INR 400-450 cr.
- **Peak revenue (by end-FY28):** ~INR 7,500-7,700 cr.
- **Debt repayment:** INR 100-125 cr payout/year; no big new debt planned; INR 1,500 cr is peak gross debt.
demand: Robust and recovering. Post-war volatility briefly disturbed downstream buyers but demand "back to base" and "very robust." Structural driver = consumer shift toward man-made / versatile fibres. Export sentiment improving (garments, home textiles) on easing tariffs and global sourcing diversification toward India. Cotton demand held up well despite sharp price escalation.
segment detail (polyester / cotton / tec:
- **Polyester filament yarn:** crude-linked; spreads good pre-war, compressed during war as RM (PTA/MEG) spiraled; pass-through stabilizing — "in process of passing on the entire hike." Mgmt cautiously constructive.
- **Cotton yarn:** significant uptick in yarn prices in Q4 on sharp spot raw-cotton rise + manufacturing-capacity disruption; margins up; FY27 raw-cotton availability a key watch (climate risk).
- **Technical/specialty yarn:** Silvassa capacity doubling; higher-value applications; growing focus area.
- No material polyester↔polyester-cotton blending shift expected from cotton price rise.
growth / optionality: Technical-textile doubling (Jul'26); Punjab Phase-2 (FY28, →INR 4,000 cr); MP cotton spindle expansion (50-acre PM MITRA plot with spare land for future). Possible forward integration / new growth leg — "concrete internal plans" hinted but not disclosed ("we will come back to you"). Exports ~5% of Silvassa volume; to rise on Silvassa but flat at consol level (Punjab serves North domestic).
margins & cost: Consol margin recovery driven by Punjab operating leverage / fixed-cost absorption as it ramps from 80-85% (Q1 FY27) toward Silvassa-like full utilization; product-mix realignment (eliminating low-fit products, adding value-added) completes through Q1 FY27 — full benefit visible from **Q2 FY27**. Solar: 32 MW hybrid solar from Serentica over 3 phases (Jul'26 → ~15 months), 3-year payback, benefit mainly FY28. Punjab uses agri-waste (no gas exposure); Silvassa gas cost up 50-60%.
capex: Punjab Phase-1 capitalized in FY26 (largest expansion in company history) — driving higher depreciation/finance cost this year. Phase-2 in works (orders to be announced), commission end-FY28. Technical-yarn doubling at Silvassa. MP cotton: INR 26 cr land + spindle capex (amount not disclosed). Solar via PPA (Serentica), not owned capex.
capital allocation (ipo proceeds): Disciplined: deleveraging INR 100-125 cr/yr; no large new debt; gross debt peaked at INR 1,500 cr. ECB in Euros fully hedged for loan tenure. Currency largely neutral (import-export natural balance + booking policy). Funding capacity expansion (Phase-2, technical, MP cotton) from internal accruals + measured debt.
risks:
- **Commodity:** crude-linked PTA/MEG volatility for polyester; pass-through lags in high volatility. Raw-cotton price/availability + climate risk for cotton. Gas cost up 50-60% at Silvassa.
- **PTA supply:** domestic GAIL & Indian Oil PTA plants delayed (GAIL paraxylene tied up by West Asia crisis → supply from Jul'26; IOC year-end) — domestic PTA price relief deferred to H2 FY27. PTA import-duty waiver status quo uncertain (could revert to 5%).
- **Demand / geopolitical:** West Asia war disrupted supply chains, spreads, downstream demand; "global environment fluid."
- **Chinese competition:** not explicitly raised; broader import-substitution / FTA tailwind is the offset.
- **Execution:** Punjab margin/value-add ramp dependent; working-capital normalization to be proven.
mgmt tone: Confident but deliberately conservative on margin %. Emphasizes EBITDA-per-ton over %; "rock solid" base operations during largest-ever expansion. Three FY27 pillars: operational stabilization & disciplined execution; improving demand/export environment; clear scalable growth road map. Repeatedly cautious on global/war situation.
non-obvious points:
- Punjab realization is at a small discount to standalone — but mgmt clarifies standalone blends in higher-priced cotton & technical yarn; pure filament gap is small (coarser North yarns + freight arbitrage deliberately shared with customers). NOT distress discounting.
- Mgmt does **not** track per-vertical (polyester/cotton/technical) P&L individually — no segment bifurcation given.
- Silvassa runs at ~95% (its optimal/"stressed" level) across all three yarns.
- Payable-days spike (59→104) is an artifact of partial-year Punjab COGS base + INR 180 cr RM-in-transit — expected to normalize, not a structural negative-WC improvement.
- Phase-2 timeline corrected mid-call from FY27 to FY28.
challenges → beneficiaries:
| Challenge / structural shift | Potential beneficiary |
|---|---|
| Man-made-fibre consumption shift + India-UK/EU FTAs + China+1 sourcing | Indian integrated yarn makers (Sanathan ✅) |
| Domestic PTA capacity (GAIL/IOC) coming on stream H2 FY27 | Polyester yarn spinners (RM cost relief) ⭐ |
| Cotton price spike + capacity disruption | Integrated cotton-yarn players with inventory discipline |

hero.oneLiner: One of India's most integrated and diversified yarn manufacturers, operating across three verticals - polyester filament yarn, cotton yarn and yarns for technical textiles - from Silvassa and a new greenfield plant at Wazirabad, Punjab.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: One of India's most integrated and diversified yarn manufacturers, operating across three verticals - polyester filament yarn, cotton yarn and yarns for technical textiles - from Silvassa and a new greenfield plant at Wazirabad, Punjab.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Sanathan Textiles manufactures yarn across three largely unrelated verticals: polyester filament yarn (made through a fully integrated setup that converts raw material into polyester chips and then into yarn), finer-count compact cotton yarn, and specialised yarns for technical textiles engineered for high durability and tenacity. The Company sells through an extensive agent-based distribution network in India and international markets, serving apparel, home textile, automotive, defence, logistics, travel and sports/athleisure customers. It is transitioning from a predominantly single-location operation at Silvassa to a multi-location footprint spanning Silvassa and Wazirabad, Punjab, with the Punjab plant run through wholly owned subsidiary Sanathan Polycot Private Limited.

- **Capacity / capex:** Technical-yarn at Silvassa doubling 9,000 → 18,000 MTPA, commissioning **end of Q1 FY27 (July)**, adds ~INR 150 cr revenue. - **Peak revenue (by end-FY28):** ~INR 7,500-7,700 cr.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- As utilisation improves, management expects stronger operating leverage, better absorption of fixed costs and a corresponding improvement in margins
- Having largely completed the peak-investment phase, the Company expects operating leverage from higher utilisation, backward integration and a progressively cleaner, lower-cost energy mix to support margins and cash flows as the new assets mature
- The Punjab commissioning raised depreciation and finance costs, temporarily impacting consolidated profitability; management frames these as transitional effects of a business that has fundamentally become stronger, with standalone operations continuing to deliver steady growth
- Incremental volumes from Punjab were absorbed across the North Indian textile market during the year, broadening the customer base and improving responsiveness across key textile clusters
- Structural shift in the fibre mix toward man-made fibres, with the Government's National Fibre Scheme seeking to rebalance India's fibre mix by 2030-31 - said to augur well for a company with capabilities across both cotton and man-made fibre yarns
- Business sentiment strengthened during the second half of FY26, particularly across export-oriented segments such as garments and home textiles, and exports of man-made yarn, fabrics and made-ups increased
- Improving export sentiment, favourable trade agreements and continued diversification of global sourcing towards India are expected to support sustained industry growth
- Near-term outlook aided by supportive policy, including the temporary exemption of raw cotton imports from customs duty and the Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Cess, and improving trade access for Indian textiles
- Polyester filament yarn is the dominant revenue driver, contributing 82% of revenue in the year, with technical textiles described as currently a smaller part of the portfolio but a significant growth opportunity
- Silvassa's proximity to India's western ports serves imported feedstock and export shipments, while Punjab serves North India through shorter lead times and logistics efficiency
- Directors remain confident in the medium-term growth trajectory while recognising that outcomes remain subject to raw-material and energy-cost volatility and to global trade and tariff developments
- Externally, elevated tariffs imposed by the United States created stress for Indian manufacturers, particularly exporters, and trade fragmentation and geopolitical tension (including the conflict in West Asia) remain sources of near-term uncertainty

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: FY 2025-26 was the year Sanathan Textiles moved from a predominantly single-location operation at Silvassa to a two-plant footprint. The greenfield polyester filament yarn facility at Wazirabad, Punjab - built and operated through the wholly owned subsidiary Sanathan Polycot Private Limited - had its continuous polymerisation line commissioned on August 27, 2025, was ramped up and stabilised at 700 MTPD, and registered that maximum capacity in the last week of March 2026, completing Phase 1 at 255,500 MTPA of polyester yarn capacity on an 80-acre site. The Company describes this as the most significant operational milestone in its history and as its first expansion of this scale accomplished in a single step; it was preceded by years of study of the North Indian textile ecosystem, and the plant is positioned to remove the freight, lead-time and working-capital disadvantage that North Indian buyers previously bore when served over long distances. Silvassa, a 50-acre site with 21 years of operation, continues to run its integrated polyester, cotton and technical-textile lines at optimal utilisation, serving domestic and export demand through proximity to India's western ports. The Company frames the journey as one from 4,500 MTPA to 479,250 MTPA built over two decades of demand-led, incremental capacity creation - understanding the market first and building second. Three further steps are disclosed in the capacity status table: an additional 9,000 MTPA of technical textiles at Silvassa where plant and machinery is installed and commissioning is pending; Phase 2 at Punjab adding 91,250 MTPA of polyester yarn capacity; and 73,000 spindles of cotton yarn capacity in Madhya Pradesh, both listed as upcoming capacity expansion. On completion of Phase 2 the Company expects aggregate installed capacity to increase substantially and polyester filament yarn capacity to more than double over the coming years. The Directors state that the peak-investment phase has largely been completed and that no dividend was recommended because capital is being deployed across the Punjab, Silvassa and Madhya Pradesh projects. Alongside capacity, investment continues in automation - automated warehousing, material handling and packing, process control, digital quality monitoring - which the Company argues is a precondition for holding its cost position at this scale, and in sustainable infrastructure: ZLD systems and rice husk / agricultural-waste biomass-fired heaters at Punjab, planned solar power initiatives, and dedicated investments in renewable generation capacity said to be at an advanced stage, with the Punjab biomass model being evaluated for replication across other sites. No rupee capex quantum is stated: the capital-commitments disclosure in this bundle is only a cross-reference to another note and carries no figure.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Three verticals with largely unrelated demand drivers - polyester economics track PTA/MEG and crude, cotton follows an agricultural rhythm, technical textiles follow industrial activity and safety regulation - so the cycles tend to offset one another and steady the earnings base
- Full forward and backward integration in polyester, converting raw material into chips and then yarn, giving control of quality at the polymer stage, a wider product portfolio from the same asset base, faster sampling and retention of value that would otherwise accrue to intermediate suppliers
- Distribution depth built over two decades - 300+ agents across 17 Indian states plus an international network, 1400+ customers serviced and 50,000+ SKUs - which let new Punjab capacity be placed through channels that already existed rather than building market and plant simultaneously
- Value-added and specification yarns (cationic dyeable, born dyed, stretch, moisture-wicking, recycled Reviro) sold on relationship and consistency rather than day-to-day price, including protective-equipment applications where qualification takes an extended period
- Punjab plant removes a structural freight, lead-time and working-capital disadvantage for North Indian buyers previously served over long distances; Silvassa's proximity to western ports serves export and imported feedstock flows
- Automation across doffing, warehousing, material handling and packaging with digital process controls and real-time quality monitoring, supporting cost optimisation at scale
- Demand-led capacity sequencing - capacity built against demand already identified, which the Company credits for holding utilisation through demand shocks, feedstock volatility and disrupted logistics

other.body:
